I’ve been farming this land in Quzhou for over forty years, and I know every corner of my fields. I’m 65 now, and my back isn’t what it used to be, but my hands still remember the work. I have six mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I’ve learned not to gamble with it. The double-cropping system of winter wheat followed by summer maize has fed my family reliably for decades, and I see no reason to change that this year.

My winter wheat went into the ground last October, and now that spring has arrived, it’s already greening up. I use improved Jimai varieties—they’re not the newest hybrids the young extension agents always push, but they’re hardy, familiar, and the seed is affordable. I’ll give the wheat four irrigations: one to protect it through the last cold snaps, then at jointing, heading, and grain-filling. I’ll spread about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, split between the reviving stage and jointing, plus 6 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium as base fertilizer. I ploughed the land before sowing last autumn, as I always do for wheat—it breaks up the corn stubble and buries the weeds. I expect around 450 kg per mu if the weather cooperates. I’ll spray pesticide twice: once for aphids in spring and once for fungal diseases before heading.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I won’t waste a single day. I’ll hire the rotary tiller to chop the wheat stubble and prepare the seedbed quickly, then plant hybrid summer maize the same week. Hybrid maize seed costs more, but the yield jump is undeniable—this is where I spend my money. I’ll irrigate twice: right after sowing to ensure emergence, and again at the grain-filling stage in August when the heat is brutal. I’ll apply 15 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 3 kg potassium per mu. Two pesticide sprays will handle the corn borers and leaf blight that always come in July and August. I’m counting on 550 kg per mu from the maize.

I thought about planting some vegetables on a corner plot for extra cash, but at my age, the labor and market hassle aren’t worth it. My nephew drives the combine, I handle the fertilizers and irrigation scheduling, and we sell the grain to the local grain station. It’s a simple, honest plan. I don’t chase miracles; I chase consistency.
